newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Disaster faces Zaire refugees as aid workers flee.
newsitem.headline: Disaster faces Zaire refugees as aid workers flee.

text.p: Disaster loomed on Saturday for a million refugees in anarchic eastern Zaire after the last outsiders who had cared for them fled for their lives.

Just over 100 foreign aid workers used a lull in the fighting for control of Goma, until this week the nerve centre for the world's biggest relief operation, to dash across the border to the Rwandan town of Gisenyi.
Zairean Tutsi rebels, backed in Goma at least by Rwandan government forces, seized towns on a 250-km (150-mile) stretch of east Zaire from rag-tag Zairean troops and Hutu allies in a two-week blitz.

In Goma on Saturday night, Reuters photographer George Malala said the fight continued for the region's biggest city -- which was a key base for the Zairean army. But much of the centre was in the hands of the Rwandans and Tutsi rebels.
The fighting, which on Friday had raged across the border to Gisenyi, had moved further away and calmed somewhat.
Aid workers arriving in Gisenyi said leaving behind the 1.1 million Hutus, who fled Rwanda and Burundi after Tutsi rivals took control, was one of the hardest decisions of their lives.
"They're on their own," Panos Moumtzis of the U.N. refugee agency, UNHCR, told British Broadcasting Corporation radio.
"With our departure there is not a single relief worker in the entire eastern Zaire region," he said. "The prospects for the Rwandans and the Zaireans are disastrous."
Tens of thousands of Zaireans caught up in the fighting have become refugees themselves.

Diplomatic efforts to find a solution to the long-feared calamity have hardly got off the ground. A regional African summit is scheduled to be held in Kenya on November 5 but Zaire says it will not attend.

France's influential Le Monde newspaper said the European Union was considering opening "humanitarian corridors" in Zaire, guarded by troops possibly from France, Belgium and South Africa, to help the refugees.
Hundreds of thousands of people are on the move across inhospitable terrain and volcanic rock in the east.
Some refugees are now dying of hunger, aid workers say.
Mark Richardson of CARE International said his aid agency had had contact with a radio operator who fled with a group of about 20,000 Rwandan refugees from the Zaire camp of Katale.
"He said they have just sat down to die. They have had no water for four or five days. These are the old, the sick, the vulnerable, the children," said Richardson in Nairobi.
The camp of Mugunga, west of Goma near the scenic shores of Lake Kivu, is the world's biggest refugee city where some 400,000 Rwandan exiles are waiting for salvation or death.
Among them are thousands of armed Hutus who were behind the 1994 genocide of up to a million Tutsis and other victims.
Frank Cawkwell of CARE-Australia, the last foreigner to quit Mugunga a couple of days ago, said all remaining food -- enough for seven days -- was being handed out to stop looting.
Aid workers fear that cholera and dysentery, the fastest killers in such desperate conditions, could soon return.
In 1994, some 50,000 Hutus died in their makeshift camps after fleeing Rwanda, fearing that the Tutsis who had won the civil war would seek revenge for the genocide.

The latest conflict in eastern Zaire, which shares a border of lakes, rivers and land with tiny Burundi and Rwanda, flared when Zairean officials told local Tutsis -- seen by Zaire as foreigners despite a centuries-long history here -- to get out.
The Tutsis fought back, with the help of Rwanda's army. Zaire says Burundi and Uganda are also behind the uprising.
Tutsis took control of Bukavu, a lakeside border town further south, and were on Saturday imposing their authority, posting guards at shops and warning looters would be hanged.
Reuters photographer Corinne Dufka saw corpses littering the streets after two days of fighting in the week. Body counts by priests and journalists suggest that at least 83 people died.
The rebel successes in the east of vast, chaotic Zaire -- 77 times the size of its former master, Belgium -- have sent shockwaves westwards to the far-away capital Kinshasa.
In a sign of internal rowing, the army accused its own government of not doing enough to help it repel the Tutsis.
Meanwhile unstable Zaire's rudder, ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, was seen up and about in a luxury Swiss hotel where he has been since an operation for prostate cancer in August.
